sentences.text: The skull of this reptile held 11 teeth in the upper jaw, 4 in the front upper jaw, and 12 in the lower jaw.
It possessed a tail fluke, nostrils positioned toward the front of the head, and keeled scales designed to assist with swimming.
This animal is one of the few Turonian mosasaurs known to have a transatlantic distribution.
Fossils from the Dukamaje Formation include vertebrae from individuals of different growth stages.
The genus was first named by Miguel Telles Antunes in 1964.
Antunes originally described the group based on a partial skull and skeleton found that same year.
Fieldwork conducted between 2005 and 2009 uncovered at least two new skeletons of the animal.
Later, CT scans of the type skull and a new skull revealed detailed interior braincase structures.
Researchers hypothesize that Angolasaurus had dark dorsal patterning to help with thermoregulation due to cooling sea temperatures.
Angolasaurus belongs to the family Mosasauridae.
It is classified as a reptile.
The parent group of Angolasaurus is Russellosaurina.
The animal is considered basal to the clade containing Tylosaurinae and Plioplatecarpinae but belongs to neither subfamily.
In 1994, the species was synonymized with Platecarpus bocagei by Lingham-Soliar.
Fossils of Angolasaurus date from the Turonian to the Coniacian stages.
Remains of Angolasaurus have been found in Angola, the United States, Brazil, and Niger.
The species Angolasaurus bocagei is known exclusively from the Itombe Formation.
Angolasaurus fossils have been recovered from the Eagle Ford Formation in Texas.
Two individuals from the Eagle Ford Formation of Texas were assigned to Angolasaurus in 2007.
It is debated whether Angolasaurus fossils from the United States, Brazil, and Niger definitively belong to this genus.
